verdict.reasoning: Patient reports feeling ‘very sort of breathless’ and ‘whenever I… breathe deeply, it sort of catches in the right hand side of my back’ and confirms this has been going on ‘Just a day, really.’
Same as cc-001: shortness of breath and right-sided back pain on deep inspiration for ‘Just a day, really.’
Patient: ‘I coughed up a bit of blood on two occasions.’ This supports cough with two episodes of hemoptysis.
Patient: ‘I’ve got a bit of a slight fever’ and ‘With the back of my hand, yes’ when asked if she measured temperature, indicating subjective, unmeasured fevers.

Patient: ‘I sort of feel my heart beating’ (palpitations), ‘I’ve been feeling a bit like a bit tired at work… exercising has been a bit difficult… performing daily activities has been a bit harder than usual’ for ‘a couple of weeks or so.’

Doctor asks about long-haul flight: ‘Have you been on any long haul flight recently?’ Patient: ‘No.’ Doctor: ‘Have you ever had any clots in your legs or clots in your lungs…?’ Patient: ‘Not that I know of, no.’ This supports no DVT/PE history and no recent long‑haul travel.
Patient: ‘I’ve got sle.’ Doctor repeats: ‘Sle. Okay.’ This indicates systemic lupus erythematosus.
Patient: ‘Yeah. Methotrexate…’ Doctor: ‘Okay… When was the last time you had methotrexate?’ Patient: ‘This morning.’
Doctor: ‘Do you have any allergies to any medication?’ Patient: ‘No.’ Doctor: ‘Any other allergies at all?’ Patient: ‘No.’ This supports no drug or other allergies.
Doctor: ‘Anyone in the family have that?’ (referring to clots). Patient: ‘No.’ This supports family history negative for clotting disorders.
Doctor: ‘Do you smoke at all?’ Patient: ‘No.’
Patient: ‘I work in an office. Just a desk job.’
Doctor: ‘Do you live alone?’ Patient: ‘Yes.’ ‘In a flat or a house?’ ‘Flat.’ ‘Do you have any pets?’ ‘Cats?’ Doctor: ‘A cat. Okay.’ This supports living alone in a flat with a cat.
After counting pulse, Doctor: ‘that was about 11 or 12. So that would make your heart rate about 66 to 74. That’s okay.’ This supports a regular pulse approximately 66–74 bpm.
During capillary refill check, patient comments ‘You’ve got very good circulation.’ Doctor: ‘Okay, perfect. That’s great.’ No delay or abnormality is mentioned, implying normal capillary refill.

Doctor performs throat inspection: ‘That’s fantastic… Perfect. Thank you for that. Excellent,’ but does not explicitly state that the throat appeared normal, only that the view/effort was acceptable. ‘Throat appeared normal’ is not stated.
Doctor: ‘tell me whether you can feel any enlarged glands or not.’ Patient: ‘No, they feel pretty normal to me.’ This supports cervical nodes not enlarged on self‑palpation.

Symptoms: shortness of breath, pleuritic right‑sided back pain, hemoptysis, fever are all described. Doctor: ‘this sounds like you might have a chest infection… we do need to assess you to figure out whether you have a pneumonia or chest infection.’ Doctor asks about flights and clots, indicating consideration of PE, but later focuses on infection, so PE is comparatively less likely.

Transcript notes SLE on methotrexate but nowhere does the doctor explicitly describe this as ‘immunosuppression with increased infection risk.’ That interpretation is clinically reasonable but not stated.
Patient: ‘But we don’t think I’m dying of lung cancer.’ and ‘you start coughing up blood and you think you’re gonna die of lung cancer.’ This shows anxiety regarding lung cancer.

Doctor: ‘we’ll arrange for you to get reviewed in a clinic today… someone to listen to your chest and maybe check your blood pressure as well and check that you’re stable… recheck your pulse as well… Check your temperature.’ This matches urgent in‑person review for auscultation, BP, pulse, temperature.

Doctor mentions possible need for investigations only in relation to excluding lung cancer and specifically a ‘follow up chest X ray,’ but does not mention a broader ‘further workup… such as chest X-ray and laboratory tests.’ Lab tests are not discussed, and workup is conditional, not a defined plan.

Doctor: ‘You may need an antibiotic.’ and later: ‘I’m not going to prescribe anything for you now because I think you need to have that basic assessment first before we proceed to the next step. But that’s what I would predict the next step might be.’ This implies starting antibiotics if pneumonia/chest infection is diagnosed.

Doctor reassures: ‘That’s not usually how lung cancers present… at the moment, it seems more like a chest infection rather than a lung cancer.’ and ‘we may end up having to do a follow up chest X ray if things don’t settle down.’ This matches reassurance, monitoring, and arranging CXR if symptoms persist.
Doctor: ‘I’m going to leave the number in the notes… for you to ring our support team and then they will book you in for a face to face appointment.’
